summary: Identifies major factors affecting the scalability of routing and basic principles for designing scalable routing for large networks. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Big road networks get hard to navigate. These are tips for keeping the map manageable as it grows.

subtitle: Design principles for routing systems that grow without collapsing.

tldr.problem: Large Internet service provider networks face two main scaling challenges: routers consume excessive resources processing routing updates, and managing routing becomes complex, both of which can cause network instability.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC outlines six design principles: build routing hierarchies to reduce router adjacencies, compartmentalize routing domains to isolate failures, make conscious trade-offs between redundancy and scalability, reduce routing information processing burden, define manageable routing policies, and use out-of-band systems to offload heavy routing tasks.
tldr.outcome: Networks can design routing systems that scale to thousands of routers and tens of thousands of routes without experiencing routing meltdowns.

today: RFC 2791 is an Informational memo describing design practices from the year 2000. While specific numbers and technology details have evolved, the core architectural principles—hierarchy, compartmentalization, aggregation, and policy simplification—remain foundational to modern ISP network design. Subsequent RFCs have built upon these principles (such as RFC 2796 on Route Reflection and later work on MPLS and segment routing).

sections.title: Routing Scalability as a Critical Problem
sections.content:
Routing is the system by which networks decide which path each data packet should take. In a large network—such as an ISP's backbone spanning multiple regions and serving thousands of customers—routing is not just important, it is essential for stability and performance.

When routing does not scale, the entire network suffers. Routers may run out of processing power, updates may propagate slowly, or the system may lose the ability to converge (reach a stable state) at all. This RFC identifies the major factors that affect routing scalability and proposes a set of design principles for building large networks that route efficiently without experiencing these failures.
sections.plainLanguage: If your city's traffic system works with a thousand cars, it might fail with a million. This document explains how to redesign it so it still works when it gets much bigger.

sections.title: Scaling Issues in Today's Large Networks
sections.content:
Today's large networks have several characteristics that create scaling challenges: hundreds to thousands of routers, rich connectivity (many redundant paths), default-free routing (knowing all approximately 70,000 routes on the Internet), and customer aggregation points with hundreds of customer routers attached to a single provider router.

Two main scaling problems arise. Router resource consumption: when network topology is unstable (links flapping up and down), interior routing protocols (IS-IS, OSPF) and exterior routing (BGP) both send many updates, consuming all available CPU on routers and preventing convergence. Routing complexity: managing sophisticated routing policies and filtering for such large numbers of routes and paths is difficult and error-prone, leading to service degradation.
sections.plainLanguage: When a road is broken and cars keep rerouting, every traffic light has to recalculate. If there are too many cars rerouting too often, the lights get overloaded.

sections.title: Building Routing Hierarchy
sections.content:
The primary solution is to build hierarchical routing: divide the network into tiers. Most networks use a two-tier design with a transit core (central backbone) and multiple access networks (regional networks) connected to it. This design can be implemented in several ways:

One approach treats the core and each region as separate administrative domains (AS), each running its own interior routing, and exchanging routes via BGP between domains. Another approach keeps everything in one AS but uses hierarchical areas in the interior routing protocol plus BGP hierarchy (route reflectors or confederations) for exterior routing. The key benefit is that instability in one region does not directly affect the entire network.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one giant traffic system, make smaller regional systems that talk to a central hub. If one region has a problem, only that region is affected.

sections.title: Reducing Routing Information Processing
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several concrete ways to reduce the burden on routers. Place routing intelligence at the edge: perform policy checks and filtering on customer aggregation routers rather than core routers, since the core carries the most traffic. Use CIDR and route aggregation: summarize customer prefixes so the core network only sees a few large blocks instead of thousands of individual routes. Utilize default routing at branch networks when appropriate; this eliminates the need to carry full Internet routing tables. Reduce alternative paths: while redundancy is important, not every destination needs dozens of alternate paths.

Another key technique is to minimize route flapping (frequent instability)—the RFC recommends route dampening, which suppresses frequently changing routes for a time to let the network stabilize.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of telling every traffic light about every road in the world, just tell the important intersections. Tell branch roads about their own area and one route out, not every possibility.

sections.title: Scalable Routing Policy and Out-of-Band Processing
sections.content:
Routing policy determines which paths traffic takes. The RFC advises making policies simple and automatable rather than complex and manual. For filtering, use autonomous system (AS) based rules for high-level decisions, and prefix-based filtering only where necessary for protecting routing integrity.

A powerful technique is to offload heavy routing tasks to out-of-band systems—separate computers that process routing information, build forwarding tables, apply policies, and filter routes, then send clean routing information to the routers. Examples include route servers at network exchange points. This approach frees routers to focus on forwarding packets rather than heavy routing computations.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of having every traffic controller make complex decisions, have one central office decide the policies, then send simple instructions to each controller.

sections.title: Practical Network Design for Scale
sections.content:
The RFC recognizes that protocol design, implementation, and network design all affect scalability. Network engineers have direct control over network design decisions and should focus on the principles outlined: hierarchy, compartmentalization, trade-offs, reduced processing, simple policies, and out-of-band assistance.

Even with new technologies like MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) and DWDM (Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing), the fundamental IGP/BGP routing model is expected to persist. Therefore, these design principles remain applicable. The document concludes that routing scalability is not a solved problem and requires ongoing attention from implementors and network architects.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no magic bullet. Building a big scalable network requires careful planning: dividing it into regions, automating policies, and using helper computers to do the heavy routing work.
